description:
🚀 We are an enthusiastic team participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge at Zewail City, Giza. We are passionate about space, technology, and innovation, and believe in teamwork, creativity, and learning together.

We welcome motivated participants with skills in programming, AI, data analysis, web development, UI/UX design, astronomy, or presentation. Beginners are welcome too!

Join us, share your ideas, and let's explore the universe together! 🌌
summary: Lunar missions face difficulties in managing and navigation, and some of those problems are reliable landing spots, communication quality, visibility, and available solar power, all of which depend on Earth and sun positions in relation to the moon. Therefore, we created an interactive web application to help mission planners and anyone interested in astrophysics to simulate the physics controlling these scenarios by including a simulation of the Sun, Earth and Moon models with landmarks, real-time calculations and statistics to test what-if situations with either custom coordinates and angles or historical values from previous NASA missions and one CSA Canadian mission. The project uses the datasets provided by the NASA Space Apps management and external verified NASA open-source datasets.
details:
Aero-Delta is an interactive mission planning platform engineered for the NASA International Space Apps Challenge 2026, purpose-built to solve one of lunar exploration's most demanding astrodynamic puzzles: where and when to land near the Moon's south pole.

At high polar latitudes, the Sun never climbs more than 6.7° above the local horizon — a consequence of the Moon's razor-thin axial tilt of 1.543°. This grazing geometry means that shifting a landing site by just two kilometers can swing available solar power from near-continuous illumination to absolute zero. Simultaneously, Earth hovers within a few degrees of the same horizon, and lunar libration — the Moon's slow physical and optical wobble of up to ±8.1° in longitude and ±6.9° in latitude — periodically drops Earth below local crater rims and massifs, severing days-long Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication windows with no warning. These two constraints — solar power and Earth line-of-sight — must be evaluated together, in real time, across multiple candidate sites and future dates before any mission can be responsibly planned.

Aero-Delta directly addresses this need. At its core is a deterministic, zero-mock-data astronomical ephemeris engine derived from J2000 epoch Keplerian mechanics and calibrated against the NASA JPL Horizons system (coord@301). The engine computes, in real time, the topocentric elevation and azimuth of both the Sun and Earth as seen by an observer standing on the lunar surface at any chosen site and date. Solar power potential is modeled using the cosine-law irradiance formula (Peff = max(0, 1361 W/m² · sin θ⊙)), and DTE communication feasibility is resolved from the Earth vector against local terrain obstructions. A 24-iteration numerical bisection solver pinpoints sunrise, sunset, earthrise, and earthset events to within 0.36 seconds of accuracy — well within mission-critical tolerances. Independent audits against JPL Horizons confirm residual errors below 0.03° (< 1.8 arcminutes), on par with the beamwidth of X-band deep space antennas.

The platform covers 15 curated candidate sites spanning the full spectrum of lunar exploration interest: Artemis III polar targets (Shackleton Crater Rim, Malapert Massif, Peak of Eternal Light, Faustini Rim, de Gerlache Rim, Connecting Ridge), CLPS commercial targets (Nobile Crater Ridge for the VIPER rover, Cabeus Crater — the LCROSS water-ice discovery site, and the Canadian Space Agency rover candidate), and Apollo historical baselines (Mare Tranquillitatis, Fra Mauro, Hadley Rille, Descartes Highlands, Taurus-Littrow). Each site is immediately comparable in a side-by-side trade-off matrix showing sunlight percentage, Earth communication availability, power feasibility, and countdown timers to critical horizon events.

The user interface layers three distinct visualization modes over this mathematical foundation:

• Mission Planner & Synodic Timeline Canvas: An interactive 29.5-day temporal canvas plots the amber Sun elevation curve and the cyan Earth elevation curve against the 0° horizon threshold, with live event markers for the next sunrise, sunset, earthrise, and earthset. Scrubbing across the synodic month collapses a complex ephemeris query into an instant operational go/no-go assessment.

• 3D Surface Horizon Viewer: A WebGL-rendered, first-person perspective from the lunar surface places the user directly in the environment. A physically textured Sun with a double-layered radiant corona casts real-time, elongated shadows across LOLA-derived crater terrain under a 2048 × 2048 shadow map. A cyan laser beam traces the Direct-to-Earth link, turning red the instant terrain occludes the signal. Authentic 3D models of the Apollo Lunar Module and an astronaut anchor the scene to human scale. One-click camera modes — TRACK SOL, TRACK EARTH, HORIZON, SURVEY — let users instantly lock onto the body of interest.

• Interactive 3D Moon Globe & Terrain Viewer: A navigable globe supports coordinate picking and topographic contour inspection, with deep-link integration into four official geospatial platforms: NASA LROC QuickMap (South Pole Stereographic EPSG:3032, LOLA DEM Stack 3314 with live Earth shadow masks), NASA Solar System Treks Moon Trek (512 PPD laser altimetry), JPL Horizons REST API, and the Canadian Space Agency exploration archives.

A bonus Apollo Lunar Module physics-based descent simulator — complete with manual throttle, hover fuel depletion, and slope clearance mechanics — makes the platform genuinely accessible to the general public and educators, not just mission architects. The embedded animated presentation deck and academic technical whitepaper ship inside the same self-contained production bundle.

Aero-Delta is built on React 18, TypeScript, Three.js / WebGL, and Tailwind CSS, bundled with Vite into a single deployable index.html via vite-plugin-singlefile, and hosted on the Vercel Edge Network. It requires no backend, no proprietary data subscriptions, and no external API calls at runtime — all ephemeris computation runs client-side, in the browser, with 100% official data provenance and zero empirical fudge factors.

“Exploration never stops — Ad Lunam et Ultra.”
